disclaimer: Fictional teaching cases. Projects, people, dates and figures are invented; the historical names are memory aids.

castor.title: CASTOR · replace the lending system
castor.goal: Loan officers currently copy the same payment details between systems. CASTOR aims to connect those systems, reduce mistakes and make payments and checks faster.
castor.you: You are the Project Manager: organise the work, bring evidence to decisions, and involve the people with authority to decide.

s01: Before there is a project, Hopper asks you to watch Curie make a loan payment.
A payment can be correct in one system and become wrong when someone copies it.
What is the actual problem, and what evidence could justify changing it?
s02: The people responsible for business and technology meet to discuss the lending problem.
An urgent complaint does not yet explain what a project should achieve.
Which questions need answers before anyone commits money or a solution?
s03: Hopper and you prepare the first formal request to start a project.
A request needs a clear business need and someone who stands behind it.
Who is asking for the change, and what should this first document contain?
s04: CASTOR reaches the investment board, which must divide limited resources between projects.
Funding one project means resources cannot be used for something else.
What information helps the board decide whether this idea deserves further work?
s05: The team compares three ways to solve the lending problem in a Business Case.
The most attractive technology may not be the best use of money.
How do costs, benefits and risks support a recommendation?
s06: The Business Case is being discussed while the project's governing team is still taking shape.
People must know who prepares, reviews and approves important decisions.
Which authority does each person actually have at this point?
s07: Detailed requirements have accumulated; you are now writing the Project Charter.
People need a shared boundary for the project without losing themselves in every feature.
What belongs in a high-level agreement about the project?
s08: The Business Case and Project Charter are ready for formal review and signatures.
A signature means a particular person accepts a particular responsibility.
Which document is each person accepting, and in what role?
s09: The team checks whether CASTOR is ready to leave Initiating and start Planning.
Moving to another phase commits the project to more work and resources.
What evidence is needed, and how are unfinished items handled?
s10: The Planning Kick-off brings the people doing and receiving the work into one room.
A shared plan is difficult if people leave with different expectations.
What should everyone understand or agree before the meeting ends?
s11: After the kick-off, you and Gantt turn meeting notes into a usable record.
A conversation is easy to forget; decisions and actions need to survive it.
What must be recorded so someone can act later?
s12: The team decides how CASTOR will be managed and records this in the Project Handbook.
A method only helps if people can use it in this project's real circumstances.
Which working rules need to be agreed and tailored?
s13: You identify the people affected by CASTOR and consider how to involve them.
Someone with little formal authority can still make adoption succeed or fail.
Whose interests, influence and practical needs should the team understand?
s14: The team sorts business requirements and agrees how later changes will be handled.
A proposed screen or button can hide the underlying business need.
How can a need be described, checked and changed without losing control?
s15: The team agrees how to assess possible problems and handle problems that already exist.
A score only helps if people know its scale and the action it triggers.
What do likelihood and impact measure, and who follows up?
s16: Quality checks and communication rules are being planned before delivery begins.
People can follow the wrong document or miss a decision if versions and messages are unclear.
How will the team check its work and keep people informed?
s17: The Project Work Plan breaks CASTOR into work packages, tasks and dependencies.
A date is not a plan until the work and the resources behind it are understood.
What work is included, and what must happen before something else can start?
s18: The Steering Committee examines the effort and cost behind the Project Work Plan.
Person-days describe work effort; they are not the same as calendar days.
How do estimates, people and the schedule fit together?
s19: This planning scene returns to April: the team works out who must approve outsourcing.
Sending a plan to the wrong authority can delay the work even when everyone agrees on the idea.
What decision is being made, and which body has authority over it?
s20: The team explains the outsourcing approach and how it will operate in practice.
Deciding to buy a platform leaves many responsibilities and boundaries to settle.
What must be clear between the institution and the supplier?
s21: Curie helps plan how future deliverables will be checked and accepted.
A product can be delivered on time and still fail the people who must use it.
What evidence would let a user say that a deliverable is acceptable?
s22: The team connects acceptance checks to the paperwork and supplier arrangements.
Checks need a usable record and an agreed way to handle failures.
How will people prove that the agreed acceptance process was followed?
s23: The team plans a safe move from the old lending system to the new one.
Real payments must continue while systems are tested, compared and changed over.
What has to be ready before switching systems?
s24: You and Hopper discuss the plan for changing how the business works.
Installing software does not automatically change people's work or create benefits.
Who understands and organises the changes needed in everyday operations?
s25: The business prepares staff for new ways of working and future benefit measurement.
Training people and measuring improvement continue beyond technical delivery.
What must change for staff, and how will improvement be demonstrated?
s26: The team reaches the Ready for Executing gate with several planning documents.
Different documents support different decisions and may have different approvers.
What evidence shows the project is ready to begin delivery?
s27: Delivery begins with an Executing Kick-off after the planning gate.
People need to understand their commitments, including those who are not in the room.
Who must be involved before the work gets moving?
s28: Gantt and you decide how to compare actual progress with the agreed plan.
A project can look busy while drifting away from its targets.
Which measurements would reveal a problem early enough to act?
s29: The supplier is now involved, and the team reviews stakeholder engagement.
A high completion percentage can conceal one important gap.
Who is still missing information or involvement, and what does that affect?
s30: People are delivering work across organisational and supplier boundaries.
Tasks depend on decisions, information and other people's work.
What does the Project Manager need to coordinate so work can move?
s31: Deming independently examines how the project is working.
Confidence in quality needs evidence about the process as well as the product.
What evidence would support a finding, and who should act on it?
s32: Close to Release 1, the team revisits a business requirement.
A preferred implementation can be mistaken for the need itself.
What outcome does the user need, and how could it be checked?
s33: The team reviews planned work, completed work and money spent.
Spending less or completing tasks does not, by itself, show whether a project is healthy.
How do these figures distinguish cost performance from schedule performance?
s34: The project must explain its status to decision-makers on one page.
A report is useful when readers can see what needs their attention.
Which evidence, exceptions and decisions matter to this audience?
s35: The team examines a real reconciliation problem while tracking project performance.
Monitoring needs to lead to action when evidence reveals a deviation.
What happened, what does it affect, and who needs to know?
s36: An influential caller asks for extra backstop functionality.
A friendly request can still alter scope, cost, schedule and risk.
What needs to be understood before anyone promises the extra work?
s37: At a risk review, the team reassesses the possibility of losing key expertise.
A changing likelihood or impact may require a different response.
What evidence changes the assessment, and who should be involved?
s38: Eiffel brings news that the lead architect has resigned.
The team must now manage a confirmed resignation and prepare for the loss of expertise.
What changes when a possible event has happened?
s39: The Steering Committee considers the consequences of the architect's departure.
Some responses exceed the Project Manager's authority or affect wider commitments.
What decision does the committee need to make, and on what evidence?
s40: Deming checks quality during Release 2, including earlier findings and document versions.
People need trustworthy records to know whether previous problems are resolved.
How is a quality problem recorded, corrected and checked again?
s41: The supplier has not yet arranged a replacement for the architect who resigned; responsibilities are under pressure.
Contractual delivery needs and internal accountability have to be handled together.
What should each role do when supplier performance becomes a problem?
s42: Release 2 reaches acceptance, including supporting material used in operations.
A working system may still be incomplete as a usable deliverable.
What was agreed for acceptance, and what evidence is missing?
s43: The old and new systems run in parallel while staff training is still incomplete.
The system and the people both have to be ready for go-live.
What does the training gap mean for business readiness?
s44: During the parallel run, two migrated loans fail to reconcile.
A small count of failures can matter when real money and reliable records are involved.
Which acceptance criteria apply, and what would justify the next step?
s45: After go-live, the team reviews transition evidence at the Ready for Closing gate.
A running system needs stable operations, support and clear ownership.
What remains to be demonstrated before the project can enter Closing?
s46: The project team meets for its final review after delivery and transition.
People will soon leave, taking valuable knowledge with them.
What should be reviewed and captured while everyone is still available?
s47: The closing group begins a discussion of lessons and who should facilitate it.
People may avoid difficult facts when the discussion feels unsafe or biased.
What conditions help the team examine its work honestly?
s48: The group compares specific experiences and draws lessons for future work.
A useful lesson needs enough context for someone else to act on it.
Which lessons explain causes and lead to a practical change?
s49: The Project-End Report must describe results before every long-term benefit can be measured.
Finishing the project and proving its business value happen on different timescales.
What can be evidenced now, and who will measure what comes later?
s50: The governing group reviews the end-of-project record and remaining responsibilities.
Closure needs a clear account of results and work that continues elsewhere.
What is being accepted or handed over at this final review?
s51: The team completes contracts, records and other administrative closure work.
A project can stop working before its obligations and records are properly closed.
What evidence and ownership must remain after the team leaves?
s52: The story returns to Lending Operations after CASTOR has closed.
The test of the project is what changes in ordinary work once the team is gone.
What can now be observed or measured about the original business problem?

pollux.title: POLLUX · turn lending data into useful reports
pollux.goal: CASTOR supplies the lending data. POLLUX builds a portal so authorised people can view reliable exposure reports without assembling eleven spreadsheets by hand. Users' needs keep changing.
pollux.you: You remain the Project Manager. Follow both the project's governing decisions and the agile team's short cycles of building, checking and adapting.

s01: CASTOR is live, but staff still assemble reports by hand and users keep requesting changes.
Clean data alone does not provide a report that people can use.
What is the reporting problem, and which needs are still uncertain?
s02: Medici asks why he should fund a project whose exact features are not yet known.
Uncertainty about features does not remove the need to justify an investment.
What can the team commit to, and what must it learn through feedback?
s03: The team prepares POLLUX's Business Case and Project Charter.
An agile delivery approach still needs a justified purpose and agreed project boundaries.
What can be agreed now despite changing reporting requirements?
s04: POLLUX reaches its Ready for Planning gate and sets up its working roles.
A team needs clarity about both governing decisions and daily coordination.
Which responsibilities remain, and where do the agile roles fit?
s05: The team discusses agile principles before deciding how to work together.
A principle should change a practical decision, rather than just decorate a wall.
Which work creates useful value, and which work may be unnecessary?
s06: The team distinguishes the overall Project Handbook from the Development Handbook.
People need to know where project rules and development agreements are recorded.
What belongs to each document, and how do they fit together?
s07: Gantt asks how the project can have a schedule when future details will change.
People need plans at different levels of detail to coordinate and adapt.
How do the Work Items List, Release Plan and Iteration Plan relate?
s08: Einstein and the team consider technical foundations before user-facing reporting work.
Technical preparation takes capacity that could otherwise produce visible features.
How can the team balance enabling work with useful feedback from users?
s09: POLLUX checks readiness to execute and establishes the first iteration's working rhythm.
Beginning development requires shared rules, people and a realistic plan.
What must be ready for the team to start short delivery cycles?
s10: After Release 1, the team plans an iteration with limited available time.
A list of desired work is not the same as work the team can realistically undertake.
How do the goal, estimates and actual capacity shape the plan?
s11: You attend the team's Daily Stand-up during an active iteration.
The meeting's purpose affects what people discuss and how useful it is.
Who needs to coordinate here, and what would distract from that purpose?
s12: The team examines its quality checks and what it means for work to be Done.
Passing one check does not necessarily mean a work item is ready to use.
How do item-specific acceptance criteria relate to shared completion standards?
s13: The team clarifies upcoming work before discussing estimates and release planning.
An estimate is unreliable if different people imagine different work.
What needs explaining before the team can estimate or compare items?
s14: Business requests compete for position in the Work Items List.
An ordering decision shapes what users receive next and what must wait.
Which roles provide input, and who owns the prioritisation decision?
s15: At the Iteration Review, the team demonstrates completed work to stakeholders.
Progress needs to be checked against actual criteria and user needs.
What evidence supports accepting the work or changing future priorities?
s16: Near the end of the Review, people want to discuss how the iteration went.
Different conversations need different participants and a different purpose.
Which discussion belongs in a product review, and which concerns the team's way of working?
s17: The team holds its Retrospective after the Iteration Review.
Improving future work requires an honest look at the process and a practical follow-up.
What can the team change, and how will it know whether the change helps?
s18: A new iteration is under way, and the team's progress chart needs interpretation.
A chart shows a pattern; it does not explain the cause or choose a response.
What does the remaining-work trend suggest the team should investigate?
s19: The team rehearses deployment and recovery ahead of the next release.
An unsuccessful change must not leave operations without a workable system.
What evidence shows the deployment and rollback plan can actually work?
s20: Ahead of Release 3, the team reviews work completed across several iterations.
Items accepted during iterations must still fit together as a usable release.
What else needs checking before the release goes into service?
s21: Gantt combines agile delivery information with the project's formal reporting and logs.
Local team information must still support project-level oversight and decisions.
How should risks, issues, changes and decisions remain visible?
s22: Nightingale examines how the Project Manager, Business Manager and agile roles relate.
Unclear reporting lines can create conflicting instructions or leave responsibility unowned.
Who coordinates the team, who manages the project, and who represents the business?
s23: After transition into service, POLLUX reaches the Ready for Closing gate.
The agile team has delivered increments, but the project still needs a controlled ending.
What evidence and handovers are needed to enter Closing?
s24: The closing team reviews lessons after many iteration retrospectives.
Local improvements and lessons for the wider organisation serve different needs.
What can the final review add to what earlier retrospectives already learned?
s25: POLLUX reaches administrative closure and reviews the effect on reporting work.
A delivered portal and a measurable improvement are related but distinct results.
Which benefits can now be demonstrated, and who owns any follow-up?

roles.you: Organises the project day to day and brings problems to the right decision-makers.
roles.nightingale: Looks after the business outcome: whether this project creates worthwhile benefits.
roles.leonardo: Looks after what is delivered: whether the technical solution meets the agreed need.
roles.hopper: Represents the business in daily work and prepares people to use the change.
roles.medici: Looks at the investment across competing projects and available resources.
roles.curie: Represents people who do the daily work and checks whether deliverables meet their needs.
roles.deming: Independently checks how the project manages quality, using evidence.
roles.gantt: Supports planning, records, reporting and the project's administration.
roles.brandeis: Checks how personal data is used and protected.
roles.turing: Looks after information security: access, integrity and availability.
roles.tesla: Designs the technical structure of the solution as part of the project team.
roles.lovelace: Turns business needs into requirements that the technical team can understand.
roles.eiffel: Coordinates the supplier's delivery and commitments to the project.
roles.einstein: Examines how the solution fits the wider technical architecture.
roles.gutenberg: Looks after documents, versions, retention and the archive.
roles.lamarr: Builds and tests software as a member of the agile team.
roles.babbage: Builds the data-related parts of the solution as a member of the agile team.

pollux_roles.curie: Owns the Work Items List and its priorities; checks work against the business need.
pollux_roles.lovelace: Helps the agile team coordinate, runs its ceremonies and removes obstacles.
pollux_roles.einstein: Guides technical architecture within the agile team.
pollux_roles.eiffel: Contributes to building, testing and planning as an agile team member.

terms: PM²
A project-management method covering roles, phases, decisions and supporting documents.
ESM
European Stability Mechanism: the institution used as the setting for these fictional projects.
LOS
Lending Operations System: the old software used to manage loans in CASTOR.
disbursement
Paying an agreed amount of a loan to the borrower.
reconciliation
Comparing records or amounts to check that they agree, and explaining differences.
exposure
Here, the amount at risk or outstanding in lending, viewed by country or other categories.
value date
The day the money must actually arrive in the receiving account.
person-days
Work effort: one person working for one day. This is not the same as elapsed calendar time.
baseline
An agreed version of a plan used as the reference for checking changes and performance.
artefact
A project document or record, such as a plan, report, checklist or log.
stakeholder
A person or group that affects the project or is affected by it.
deliverable
A product or result the project must produce and hand over.
benefit
A measurable improvement resulting from the project's outcome.
Business Case
The justification for the project: the problem, options, costs, benefits and risks.
Project Charter
The high-level agreement about the project's purpose, scope, objectives and organisation.
scope
The boundary of the work and results included in the project.
RfP
Ready for Planning: the decision point before moving into Planning.
RfE
Ready for Executing: the decision point before moving into Executing.
RfC
Ready for Closing: the decision point before moving into Closing.
PSC
Project Steering Committee: the group that oversees the project and makes important project decisions.
AGB
Appropriate Governance Body: the higher-level body concerned with the organisation's investment decisions.
Business Implementation
Preparing the business to use the project's results and realise the expected benefits.
transition
Moving the delivered solution into operational use, with ownership and support in place.
iteration
A short cycle of planning, building and checking work; two weeks in POLLUX.
release
A set of work made available for use; it may bring together several iterations.
Work Items List
The ordered list of work the agile team may undertake.
WIL
Work Items List. A number such as WIL-127 identifies one item, not an amount of work.
PrOw
Product Owner: the agile role that owns and prioritises the Work Items List.
TeCo
Team Coordinator: the agile role that facilitates the team and its working process.
ArOw
Architecture Owner: the agile role that guides the technical architecture.
ATeM
Agile Team Member: someone who helps plan, build and test the solution.
acceptance criteria
The specific conditions used to check whether a work item or deliverable meets the agreed need.
Definition of Done
The team's shared completion and quality standards that work must meet.
enabler
Technical or supporting work that makes later business functionality possible.
retrospective
A meeting where the team examines and improves its way of working.
burn-down
A chart showing how much planned work remains over time.
rollback
Returning to the previous working state if a deployment fails.
risk
An uncertain event that could affect the project if it occurs.
issue
A current problem that needs attention and a response.
